R08-B-01: Few school subjects have lost their defenders as quickly as handwriting. When most adult writing passes through a keyboard or a touchscreen, the hours once devoted to forming letters on lined paper can look like a ritual preserved out of institutional habit rather than educational necessity. Why, the argument runs, should a child labour over the loops of a joined script that she will rarely use after leaving school, when the same time could be given to typing, programming or simply reading more widely? The objection has the considerable appeal of common sense, and part of it is right. But it rests on a narrow idea of what handwriting lessons were ever for. The narrow idea treats handwriting as a delivery system, a way of getting words from a head onto a surface, and judged by that standard alone it has plainly been outpaced. Yet for a young child, forming a letter by hand is also a way of learning the letter. To write a b rather than a d, the child must attend to direction, proportion and the small differences that distinguish one shape from its neighbours, and that sustained attention seems to help fix the shapes in memory in a way that pressing a key does not. A keyboard presents every letter ready-made; the hand has to build each one. Several researchers have suggested that this building is part of how early readers come to recognise letters at all, though the evidence is still being argued over and is far from settled. There is a second, quieter benefit, which concerns older students rather than beginners. Students who take notes by hand cannot transcribe a lecture word for word, because the hand is too slow. They are forced to choose, compress and rephrase, and that compression is itself a kind of thinking, an early and private interpretation of what the lecturer actually argued. The student with a laptop can capture far more, and may understand far less, since verbatim copying can proceed without the words ever being weighed. The slowness that makes handwriting look obsolete is, in this setting, precisely its use. None of this is an argument for preserving every feature of the old curriculum. The insistence on one elegant joined style, and the marks lost for an untidy loop, had more to do with the manners of an earlier age than with learning, and they can be abandoned without much loss. Nor should typing be neglected in the name of tradition; children need both. The case for handwriting, properly made, is modest: not that it is beautiful or traditional, but that the hand teaches the eye and slows the mind in ways that are useful precisely because they are inefficient. A curriculum that drops it to save time may find that it has saved the wrong thing.
R08-B-02: The replacement of the scroll by the codex is one of the quiet revolutions in the history of reading. In the Mediterranean world of the early centuries of the common era, a book was usually a long roll of papyrus, wound on itself and read by unrolling one column at a time; within a few hundred years the dominant form had become the codex, a stack of folded sheets bound along one edge, which remains the shape of most books today. The customary explanation for the change is economy: a codex uses both sides of its writing material, it packs more text into less volume, and it is easier to carry. All of this is true, and none of it is quite enough. The economic story struggles with timing. If thrift alone had driven the change, one would expect the codex to have spread fastest where writing material was scarce and to have triumphed as soon as its savings were obvious. Instead it lingered for generations as a humble format for notebooks, accounts and school exercises, while prestigious literature stayed on the roll. Its adoption was uneven in ways that cost does not explain; some communities, early Christian ones among them, seem to have taken it up well before their neighbours, for reasons that probably had as much to do with identity and use as with price. A more illuminating difference lies in how the two forms allow a reader to move through a text. A scroll is constructed for continuous reading from beginning to end: to find a passage near the middle, one must wind through everything that precedes it, and comparing two distant passages is awkward enough that readers leaned heavily on memory instead. A codex, by contrast, can be opened anywhere. A finger can hold one place while the eye checks another; a page can be marked, numbered and returned to. The codex, in other words, made the text navigable, and navigation changed what reading could be. A legal compilation, a book of scripture to be cited in argument, a technical manual to be consulted rather than recited: these are works one enters at a point rather than travels through, and they suit the codex far better than the roll. It would be a mistake to convert this into a narrative of inevitable progress. Readers of rolls were not deprived; they cultivated habits of memorisation and recitation that served their purposes admirably, and something of that intimacy with a whole text may have been lost when books became places in which to look things up. Nor did the codex create consultative reading out of nothing. But the form encouraged certain practices and discouraged others, and over centuries the encouragement told. The later apparatus of the book, page numbers, tables of contents and indexes, would have been nearly pointless on a roll. It is the codex's logic worked out in full.
R08-B-03: When people settle an argument about a word by 'looking it up', they treat the dictionary as a court whose ruling ends the case. The image is understandable, since a dictionary speaks in the flat, confident voice of a statute, but it misrepresents how the better dictionaries are made. A serious dictionary does not decide what words mean; it reports, as carefully and as comprehensively as it can, what speakers and writers have been observed to mean by them. The method is easiest to see in the large historical dictionaries begun in the nineteenth century. Their editors did not sit down and define words from their own sense of correctness. They gathered evidence: slips of paper, many of them sent in by volunteer readers, on each of which a sentence containing a word had been copied out with its source and date. A definition was written only after the slips for a word had been sorted into piles according to the senses they seemed to show. Where the evidence was thin, the entry was thin; where a sense appeared in the slips before anyone had thought to approve of it, it went in regardless. The definition, on this model, is a summary of a body of quotations, and the quotations printed beneath it are not decoration but the grounds on which it rests. It does not follow that a dictionary is a neutral mirror. The evidence has to be collected by someone, and collectors read some kinds of text more than others; for a long time published literary prose was heavily over-represented, while the speech of the street and the workshop barely appeared. Someone must also decide where one sense ends and another begins, a judgment the slips cannot make for themselves. And the labels a dictionary attaches, such as 'informal', 'nonstandard' or 'archaic', are themselves verdicts, even when they are offered as descriptions. A dictionary that claimed to have no point of view would simply be concealing the one it has. The honest position lies between the court and the mirror. A good dictionary is an argument from evidence: its claims can be checked against the citations, and they can be revised when new evidence arrives, which is why the best dictionaries are never finished. To read one well is to notice the quotations as well as the definitions, and to treat its authority as that of a careful witness rather than a judge. That is a more modest authority than the one we usually grant it, but it is a sturdier one, since it does not collapse the first time usage moves on.
R08-B-04: Each new medium of reading arrives with a lament attached. The prevailing anxiety is that screens are making us worse readers: that a generation raised on phones can no longer follow a sustained argument, and that anything read on a device is necessarily read badly. Some of this anxiety is supported by evidence. A number of studies have reported that people tend to understand long and demanding texts somewhat less well on screens than on paper, especially when they are working against the clock. But the usual interpretation of such findings, that the screen itself damages comprehension, is too quick. Consider what readers characteristically do on screens. Most of what they encounter there is brief, and much of it is read in order to decide whether to read it at all: headlines, messages, feeds, search results. Over years, this produces a thoroughly practised habit of skimming, in which the eye hunts for familiar key words and moves on, and when the same reader is later handed a dense essay on a tablet, the habit accompanies the device. The reader skims because skimming is what that screen has always been for, and comprehension suffers accordingly. On this account the difficulty lies less in the glass than in the expectations that the glass has gradually trained. This explanation carries a more encouraging implication. Habits, unlike physiological limitations, can be changed, and some of the gaps reported in the research seem to narrow when readers are given more time, or are asked to slow down and summarise what they have read. A reader who approaches a screen with the deliberate intentions he would bring to a printed book may perform nearly as well as he would with the book itself. The underlying capacity for sustained attention is not lost; it is simply not being called upon. Yet none of this shows that the medium makes no difference at all. Paper offers a reader a sense of place that a scrolling screen does not: the thickness of the pages already read, the position of a passage on the left or right page, the feel of a chapter's length in the hand. These cues help some readers remember where an idea appeared and how a long argument is organised, and a screen supplies them only weakly. The sensible conclusion is therefore a qualified one. Screens are not destroying our capacity to read deeply, but they make it easier not to, and readers and teachers who want deep reading on screens will have to ask for it deliberately rather than expect it by default.
R08-B-05: The picture of the author that most readers carry is a picture of solitude: one person, one desk, one manuscript that emerges complete and is then merely printed. Publishing reinforces the picture at every step. The author's name alone goes on the cover, the author gives the interviews and accepts the prizes, and the acknowledgements page, where the other contributors are thanked, is the page readers most reliably skip. Yet anyone who has watched a book being made knows that the finished text is rarely the text the author first submitted. Between those two texts stands, among others, the editor. At the broadest level, an editor may tell an author that the book begins in the wrong place, that a character is doing no work, or that the argument of a long middle section has already been made in its first ten pages. At the finest level, an editor queries a word, a comma, the order of two clauses. Much of this advice is accepted, some of it is fought over and some is refused; but the book that reaches the reader has been shaped by all three outcomes, since even a rejected suggestion can force an author to articulate why a passage must stay. The work is deliberately invisible. A good edit, like good stage lighting, is meant to pass unnoticed, and editors who want their contribution celebrated are generally thought to have misunderstood the job. One tempting response is to declare that editors are secret co-authors and that the solitary author is a fraud. This overcorrects. In most cases the author supplies the material, the voice and the governing intention, and the editor works on what the author has made rather than making it; the relation resembles that between a performer and an exacting coach more than that between two composers. There are exceptions, cases in which an editor's cuts and rewritings have been so extensive that the question of whose book it is becomes genuinely difficult to answer, but they are exceptions precisely because they unsettle us. The real lesson concerns how we assign credit rather than who deserves the most of it. Our habits treat authorship as an all-or-nothing property, possessed entirely by one person, when the making of most books is a graded collaboration in which contributions differ in kind as well as in size. Recognising this would not diminish authors. It would make it easier to see what they actually do, which is not to produce text from nothing but to direct a process that others help to carry out, and to bear responsibility for the result.
R08-B-06: It has become a commonplace that printing fixed the text. Before the press, the argument goes, every copy of a work was made by hand, and every copyist introduced errors of his own, so that texts drifted further from their originals with each generation of transcription. The press ended the drift: it produced hundreds of identical copies at once, and it was this identity, more than mere abundance, that allowed scholars across a continent to cite the same page and to dispute the same words. The thesis is powerful, and in its broad outline it is not wrong. But it credits the machine with an achievement that took centuries and required far more than machinery. Look closely at the books of the hand-press period and the identical copies begin to dissolve. Printers corrected errors while a sheet was being run, stopping the press to change a letter or a line and then carrying on; the sheets already printed were too costly to waste and were bound up alongside the corrected ones. Two copies of the same edition may therefore differ on any number of pages, and it is possible that no surviving copy matches any other exactly. Reprints, authorised or not, introduced fresh errors and silent improvements of their own. To a reader of the period, a printed book was a more dependable object than a manuscript, but it was not the guaranteed replica that the commonplace imagines. What made print seem fixed, then, was less the press than a slowly assembled set of expectations and institutions around it. Legal rights over copies gave publishers a motive to suppress unauthorised versions. Scholarly editors developed procedures for collating copies and establishing a single authoritative text. Readers learned to expect that a citation to page and line would lead others to the same words, and that expectation, once widespread, pressed printers toward the consistency it presupposed. Fixity was in this sense a social achievement that the technology made possible but did not by itself deliver. The distinction matters because the same commonplace is now being run in reverse. Digital texts, we are told, are inherently unstable: they can be altered silently, updated without notice, made to differ from one reader's screen to the next. That is true of the technology, but the history of print suggests that it is not the whole story. Whether digital texts become stable will depend on whether comparable institutions grow up around them: archives that preserve versions, conventions for citing them, and readers who expect, and demand, that a text once published remains what it was. The machine sets limits; it does not settle the outcome.
R08-B-07: A library catalogue looks like the least ideological of documents. Its function, apparently, is merely to inform a reader where a particular book is located, and the call number on a spine seems as neutral as a street address. But a classification scheme does more than locate. To place a book, it must first decide what the book is about, and to do that it must divide the whole of knowledge into classes, arrange the classes in an order, and decide which subjects deserve broad territory and which can be squeezed into a corner. Every call number is, in compressed form, a small theory of what its book is about. These are not merely technical decisions. They are judgments about how the world is organised, made by particular people at a particular time, and then built, quite literally, into buildings. The judgments show most clearly where a scheme meets subjects its makers did not think central. One widely used decimal scheme, devised in the nineteenth century, gave most of the numbers in its religion class to varieties of Christianity, leaving the rest of the world's traditions to share a small remainder. Nobody needs to suppose malice to explain this; the scheme reflected the collections and the assumptions of the libraries its maker knew. But the consequence outlived the assumptions. A library using such a scheme in a city of many faiths must either cram large collections into long, unwieldy numbers or improvise local fixes that make its shelves harder to share with other libraries. The effect is not confined to how much space a subject receives. Classification also governs adjacency, and adjacency governs discovery. A reader who goes to the shelf for one book finds its neighbours, and much of what people learn in libraries they learn through this kind of sideways encounter. Suppose a hypothetical study of household labour is shelved among works on economics; its browsers will meet it as an argument about production and value. Shelved instead among works on the family, it will be met as an argument about domestic life. The book is the same, but the conversation it is placed in is not, and the scheme, rather than the author, has chosen the conversation. From this one might conclude that classification is a kind of censorship which libraries should abandon in favour of keyword search, which appears to impose no order at all. The conclusion does not follow. Search systems rank their results, and ranking embodies choices just as surely as shelving does; the choices are merely harder to see. Moreover, a collection with no arrangement is not neutral but unusable, since a reader can then find only what she already knows to ask for, whereas the browser of a well-ordered shelf may stumble on books she never knew existed. Some order is the price of a library's being useful, and every order has a point of view. The more defensible lesson is that classification should be treated as revisable and should be visible as a choice. Schemes have in fact been revised many times, often after communities pointed out how they were misdescribed, and catalogues increasingly allow a book to carry several subject headings even though it can stand in only one place. Revision is not a confession of failure but the ordinary condition of any scheme that tries to describe a body of knowledge which keeps changing beneath it. No scheme will ever be neutral. What can reasonably be asked of one is that it knows it is not, and that it leaves room for readers to cross the boundaries it draws.
R08-B-08: For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, scholars who wrote about the history of writing liked to arrange the world's scripts on a ladder. At the bottom stood picture-writing, in which signs resembled the things they named; above it came scripts in which signs stood for whole words; above those, scripts whose signs stood for syllables; and at the summit, the alphabet, in which a few dozen letters represented the individual sounds of speech. The ladder told a story of progress toward economy and abstraction, and it rarely escaped notice that the peoples occupying the topmost rung were, in most such accounts, the authors' own. The ladder has not survived scrutiny well. Its first difficulty is descriptive. The scripts it consigned to the lower rungs were seldom what it said they were: the characters of Chinese, often presented as pictures of things, are in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another indicates, however loosely, sound. Such a script is not a halting step toward phonetic writing but a different and highly developed answer to the problem of recording a language. Its second difficulty is historical. The sequence it describes is, at best, the history of one lineage of scripts in one region, and to present it as the path that all writing must follow is to mistake a family tree for a law of nature. The deeper difficulty concerns the standard of judgment. The ladder assumed that a script should be ranked by how few signs it needs, so that fewer signs meant a better system. Economy of inventory is a real virtue; a child learning an alphabet with regular spelling can sound out unfamiliar words within a few years, and few would deny that this is an advantage. But it is one criterion among several. A script that represents meaning directly can be read across spoken varieties that differ so much in pronunciation that their speakers cannot follow one another in conversation. A mixed system, such as the one used for Japanese, can show at a glance which parts of a sentence carry lexical content and which carry grammar, an aid to rapid reading once the system is mastered. And an alphabet is only as economical as its spelling permits; a language whose spelling has drifted far from its pronunciation, as English has, can oblige its learners to memorise many words almost as wholes. None of this implies that scripts are equal in every respect or that the choice of script is unimportant. The costs of learning differ, and some of them fall heavily on those with the least schooling. A script deliberately devised in fifteenth-century Korea, whose letter shapes reflect how the sounds they represent are produced, was designed with exactly such learners in mind, and its designers evidently believed that some ways of writing were better than others for certain ends. That belief is a ranking of a kind, but it is a ranking relative to a purpose, which is precisely what the ladder lacked. It is also worth noticing what the ladder's critics should not claim. To deny that the alphabet is the summit of writing is not to say that literacy rates owe nothing to scripts; they plainly owe something. It is to say that they owe much more to schools, to the availability of reading matter and to whether reading pays, and that societies with very different scripts have reached near-universal literacy once those conditions were in place. The ladder told us that the script was destiny. The record suggests it is closer to terrain: it shapes the route, but it does not decide who arrives.
